utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated. With this decision, we are going to close, I hope, two days of very hard work. Here is the decision of the Chamber. In a preliminary manner, the Chamber wishes to remind the parties that before filing a motion, regardless of its nature, except in the case of an ex parte motion, they should previously discuss amongst themselves the provisions of the motion and seek to achieve an agreement. The motion should be brought before the Chamber only in the case of persistent disagreement. Furthermore, all written motions should be filed with the Registry simultaneously in both official languages of the Tribunal, and it is the duty of the parties to undertake the necessary steps to achieve that. Finally, except in the case of unforeseeable circumstances, motions should be filed within a reasonable time frame, allowing the Chamber to be able to rule, so before the question addressed actually arises. Regarding the measures for the protection of witnesses, the Chamber wishes to recall that the Rule is that hearings be held in public. The Chamber notes that the number of witnesses for which a closed session is requested is not such as to call into question in any significant way the principle of the public nature of hearings. To the extent to which the Chamber does not have the resources for necessary inquiries, it is up to the parties to provide it with all the elements, allowing it to judge on a case-by-case basis whether it is desirable for a witness to be granted the exceptional measure which a closed session hearing constitutes. Under these conditions, the Chamber grants protective measures 1, 2, 3, 4, and 8 mentioned in paragraph 12 of the Prosecution motion, dated 27 April 2000. The Chamber also rules that the accused, his counsel, or his representatives, acting in accordance with their instructions or at their request, may not contact a witness or a potential witness of the Prosecutor, or any other person identified in the elements provided to the Defence by the Prosecutor, unless the Prosecutor has been advised of the same in writing within a reasonable time frame. In the case of such a request, the Prosecutor may be present in the event of any such meeting between the Defence and that person if the person so requests. That measure will apply on a reciprocal basis to the Defence witnesses which the Prosecutor wishes to contact. Concerning trial summaries and transcripts which the Prosecutor should like to tender into evidence, we decide that regarding the transcripts, the statements made by witnesses which the Prosecutor wishes to call again represent prior statements in the sense of Rule 66 of the Rules and should therefore be disclosed to the Defence as early as possible, and including in a language the accused understands. The Chamber feels that such a communication will occur only in exceptional circumstances, which the Prosecutor will justify, at least seven working days before the envisaged date for the appearance of the said witness. Under those circumstances, the two parties should endeavour to avoid posing to the witness the same questions to which he has already provided answers during his first appearance in order to avoid any repetition. Naturally, the Chamber will judge on a case-by-case basis, if necessary, the repetitive nature of the questions posed to see whether such a repetition is justified. Regarding trial summaries mentioned in section 2(b) of the Prosecution motion, dated 28 April 2000, the Chamber believes that this could be a measure which could speed up the proceedings. In order to form an opinion, the Chamber wishes that the Prosecutor should provide it with the trial summaries which it has already disclosed to the Defence. For the immediate future, and in order not to further delay proceedings, the Chamber authorises the Prosecutor to use those summaries orally at hearings. In order to facilitate the use of their rights by the Defence, the Chamber will consider it necessary that a draft summary should be disclosed to the Defence, including in a B/C/S version, at least seven working days prior to the date envisaged for the appearance of the witness concerned. Concerning the cross-examinations, the parties have agreed, as regards Prosecution witnesses, that after the examination-in-chief, the Defence counsel of Miroslav Kvocka will notify the Chamber the order in which the Defence counsel of the accused wish to cross-examine that witness, and the Chamber accepts this suggestion. The Chamber is of the opinion that as soon as witnesses appear before it, the witnesses are less witnesses of one party but more witnesses of justice. From that standpoint, it is important that contacts by either party with a witness should cease immediately after the solemn declaration made by the witness before the Chamber. Naturally, a party will always be able to notify the Chamber of any reasons which might justify exceptional contacts with the witness. But the principle is that all contacts should be prohibited between the parties and a witness after the witness has taken the solemn declaration, until the end of his testimony before the Chamber in the case that is being heard. Regarding an on-site visit, the Chamber has contacted the competent services to envisage the possible transport on site, as requested by the Prosecutor. At this stage, it is not able to provide an answer. Regarding judicial notice, it appears to the Chamber that it is important to fix, as of now and to the extent possible, the framework of the debates. In that context, the Chamber takes note only of the facts and only those facts on which agreement has already been reached by the parties. That is the decision of the Chamber. I would perhaps like to add that this is the ruling of the Chamber which we may review or amend if the need to do so should arise. As I have always said, we are trying to organise our work, and we are not slaves of organisation. Organisation is there to serve us, and therefore to the extent to which that organisation is going to serve our purpose, we will maintain it. If it proves not to be useful, we can reconsider it. Therefore, I think that, as I said at the beginning, we are going to close these two days of work. There will not be any written ruling. This is the decision of the Chamber and this is the definitive decision. Therefore, I think it is not appropriate or useful to bring in a witness now, so I think we will adjourn for today. Madam Hollis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution asks clarification on two points. Regarding your decision on the transcripts, you indicated that the transcripts must be disclosed seven days before the testimony. The Prosecution understands from that that with our first witness, we will not be allowed to put the transcript into evidence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The decision applies for the next few days, and for tomorrow we're going to function in accordance with the normal Rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. The second matter I'd like to raise, I believe we have to go into private session. It concerns our oral application on two witnesses for protective measures. Could we go into private session on that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we're going to go into private session, please. Mr. Marc Dubuisson, will you take the necessary steps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are now in a public session. Thank you for your attention, Mr. O'Sullivan. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: At one point in your decision, I believe I heard you say that henceforth all pleadings should be filed simultaneously in French and English. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Now, does that mean that -- there are times, and we take the example of the Prosecution's request for pseudonyms, a lengthy document, one that needs to be put out in writing for the Bench and for the parties to understand, that is going to cause considerable delays, I submit, in requiring translation. First of all, the time frame. Second of all, have arrangements been made with the Registry to provide the Defence with appropriate funding for translation services? Because some of these motions are very short. Some of them, such as final submissions, will likely be hundreds of pages long. And the intermediary example is one that we have before us on the protection of witnesses, which was lengthy, 25 pages or so, I believe, and one that will take time to prepare and translate. It's just the practicalities of that aspect of the ruling that I would like some clarification on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. O'Sullivan, we are fully aware of the implications. But one thing is sure: There are two official languages in the Tribunal. I personally prefer French, and I never have translations into French. If we begin to do that, if the motions, if the documents are filed in both languages, then we will be able to work in a different manner. I wish to say that I think it was only last Friday that I received the French translation of the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution. If I were to refuse to work in both languages, then this trial could not have begun. So that if we really begin working in both languages, I think all of us have -- in this Chamber, we are working in both languages. So after all, we have the right to work in both languages. Perhaps this will be the only Chamber working in two languages. But measures have to be taken. Whether it costs money or not, we have to adjust to this situation. Perhaps it will take time. We will adjust gradually. But we have to bear in mind that the Tribunal works in two official languages, and they have to be put in motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand quite well that there are two official languages. But there is the practical side of translating a document which is first drafted in English or in French, and I understand in principle. We do not wish to prolong things. A motion has to be submitted seven days in advance, but that will become 14 or 21 days if these things simply cannot be translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I will give you an example of what we are speaking about. If all people could speak the two languages, there are no problems. The problem exists because there are people who don't speak the two languages. So we know, we are aware, of these practical questions. But always the documents have to be translated after. Why not translate them before? It's some kind of reorganisation of the things. The money and the time we spend, we always spend the time and the money. It's a question of reorganisation, to reorganise the things, I think. So maybe all of us have to make some effort to do this. Because the pre-trial brief of the Prosecutor was translated now. Why not translate it before? So I think we have to make really sincere efforts to do this. As I said, this Trial Chamber works in two languages, and we need to work -- we have difficulties today even because we work in two languages. If we would have all the documents in French, and even in English, maybe we would succeed earlier and maybe we might have other results. But anyway, with all these difficulties, we tried, and I think we succeeded. [Interpretation] To wind up this discussion, I know that I have caused the interpreters a lot of problems by changing languages, and I apologise, but an effort needs to be made, I think. It is a decision of the Chamber which we will try to implement. I think the whole Tribunal and all the other Chambers should adopt this rule as well, because as you know, other international courts always publish and always accept documents in the official languages. It is in the Statute; it is clearly written that there are two official languages in this Tribunal. In any event, we are always available and ready to consider exceptional circumstances. I think that you know that this Chamber has published a judgement a few months ago. We still don't have the translation. I think that we have no other matters to address today, and I truly hope that we will be here tomorrow to recommence our trial at 9.30. So we will see you all tomorrow. Thank you all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: 2.25 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 4th day of May, 2000, at 9.30 a.m.
